name: german-basics

description.en: 125 basic German words and phrases for beginners: the numbers 0–20, the tens and 100, the days of the week, the months, eight colours, family members, greetings and polite phrases, and everyday nouns, adjectives and verbs. The front shows the German word in current spelling; nouns, days and months are given with their definite article (der Tisch, die Tür, das Buch). The back gives its English and Swedish meaning, or the digits for a number, with the plural of most nouns in a note. Words, genders and meanings from Wikidata's lexemes and a public-domain US Government course and phrase book (the Foreign Service Institute's German Basic Course and the War Department's German Phrase Book), checked against German and English Wiktionary, Folkets lexikon and the official German spelling rules.
description.sv: 125 grundläggande tyska ord och fraser för nybörjare: talen 0–20, tiotalen och 100, veckodagarna, månaderna, åtta färger, familjemedlemmar, hälsningar och artighetsfraser samt vardagliga substantiv, adjektiv och verb. Framsidan visar det tyska ordet i nutida stavning; substantiv, veckodagar och månader står med bestämd artikel (der Tisch, die Tür, das Buch). Baksidan ger betydelsen på engelska och svenska, eller siffrorna för ett tal, och de flesta substantiv har pluralformen i en anteckning. Ord, genus och betydelser från Wikidatas lexem och en amerikansk statlig kurs och parlör fria från upphovsrätt (Foreign Service Institutes German Basic Course och krigsdepartementets German Phrase Book), kontrollerade mot tyska och engelska Wiktionary, Folkets lexikon och de officiella tyska stavningsreglerna.

method: The research, drafting and cross-checking of this deck were done by AI agents (Claude, by Anthropic) at Anton Wiklund's direction, with machine checks against Wikidata and the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators. Quality control round 0 below is the authoring agent's own source and machine checks; review rounds by independent AI reviewers, when they have been made, are recorded after it. The cards have not yet been reviewed by a human subject expert (a teacher of German or a translator).

Word list. A list of 125 words and phrases for a first German course was drawn up by hand from the library editor's brief (numbers 0–20, the tens and 100; days; months; colours; family; greetings and polite phrases; everyday nouns, adjectives and verbs), choosing the most basic, standard word for each concept and avoiding words whose everyday form differs by region (see Excluded). No frequency list, textbook word list or phrase-book list was copied: the public-domain US Government course and phrase book below were read only for the meaning of greetings already on the list and for facts in the notes.

Wikidata lexemes. SPARQL query 1 fetched every German lexeme (language Q188) whose lemma is a candidate, with its lexical category, grammatical gender (P5185), senses, English and German glosses and sense items (P5137). Phrases not found were looked up with the lexeme search (API calls 2): Wikidata has no German lexeme for guten Tag, guten Abend, gute Nacht or auf Wiedersehen. The full JSON of the lexeme chosen for each word (the numeral lexeme for numbers, the noun lexeme for nouns, the verb lexeme for verbs, and so on) was fetched with API calls 3; it gave the nominative plural form of each noun (the form with the features plural Q146786 and nominative Q131105). The English and Swedish lexemes named by the senses' translation statements (P5972) were fetched with API calls 4, and query 7 looked for English and Swedish senses that point to the German senses.

Wikidata items. The items linked from the senses (P5137) were fetched with API calls 5 (labels and aliases in German, English, Swedish and mul). For concepts whose lexeme sense has no item (the colours red, blue, white and brown; cold; the greetings guten Tag and guten Abend) items were found with the item search (API calls 6). The items give the English and Swedish labels for numbers, days, months, colours, family members and everyday things, and the German label or alias that the builder checks against the front.

Phrases. For the greetings with no lexeme, and as a second content source for the others, a public-domain US Government course and a phrase book on the Internet Archive were read (calls 9 and 10): the Foreign Service Institute's German Basic Course (1961), whose Unit 1 basic sentences give Guten Morgen, Guten Tag ("Hello (Good day)"), Guten Abend, Auf Wiedersehen ("good bye"), danke, bitte, ja and nein with their English meaning (its Unit 4 also gives the facts behind the notes on Sonnabend, meine Frau and the possessive sein); and the War Department's German Phrase Book TM 30-606 (1943), whose greetings page gives "Good night — Gute Nacht", the only source of that card's content. The FSI text was read in the Internet Archive's OCR text; the phrase book's OCR text is poor, so its pages 10–17 were rendered from the scanned PDF with PyMuPDF (call 10) and read directly.

Writing the cards. The front is the German word in the current (post-reform) spelling, as in the lexeme's lemma. Nouns, the days and the months are capitalised and preceded by the definite article that matches the lexeme's grammatical gender (der for masculine, die for feminine, das for neuter); every gender was confirmed against German Wiktionary's Genus. Numbers, colours and other adjectives, verbs (in the infinitive) and the interjections are in lower case, as in the dictionary. The multi-word greetings are given in their dictionary form, lower case except for the noun (guten Morgen, auf Wiedersehen), as Wikidata, German Wiktionary and the official word list write them. Entschuldigung, a noun used on its own as an apology, is capitalised and has no article; its note gives the noun. Of the two official spellings tschüss and tschüs, the card uses tschüss (the Wikidata and German Wiktionary lemma) and the note names tschüs.

The back is our own short English and Swedish rendering of the main sense: for nouns the bare noun, for verbs the infinitive (English "to …", Swedish "att …"), for numbers the digits, tagged zxx (text in no language). English and Swedish follow the Wikidata labels where an item exists and its label is the everyday word; otherwise they are the standard English and Swedish equivalents chosen by the authors and checked in English Wiktionary and Folkets lexikon (step 9). Where German has one word for two English or Swedish words, both are given (Stadt: town, city; Straße: street, road / gata, väg; groß: big, large; Großvater: farfar eller morfar). Swedish uses lower case for days and months. Every text is tagged with its language: the front de, the back en and sv, digits zxx.

Notes. A short note was added where it helps a beginner and the sources confirm it: the nominative plural of countable nouns (from the lexeme form, checked against German Wiktionary; not given for Wasser, Milch, Geld and Arbeit, whose plurals are rare or have another meaning), the spelling of sechzehn, sechzig, siebzehn, siebzig and dreißig, einhundert (a Wikidata alias of 100), Sonnabend (northern and eastern Germany) and Jänner (Austria), weiß as a form of wissen, Schwester also meaning nurse, Mann also husband, Frau also wife and Mrs, Strasse in Switzerland, groß also tall, Wie geht es Ihnen?, the possessive sein, guten Tag as a daytime greeting, “see you again” as another rendering of auf Wiedersehen, tschüss as a goodbye among friends and its spelling tschüs, the other uses of bitte, and the noun die Entschuldigung. Notes are our own wording, and each note's fact comes from a content source: Wikidata (the senses husband L7302-S3, wife L2945-S2 and nurse L34032-S4 with their items; Jänner's location of sense usage, Austria; the Swiss lemma Strasse of Straße; the lexemes tschüs and possessive sein; tschüss's gloss "freundschaftlicher Verabschiedungsgruß"), the FSI course (Sonnabend in northern and eastern Germany, meine Frau for one's wife, sein Sohn, Sie as the formal address, Frau Kunze, Wie geht es Ihnen?) or the War Department phrase book ("See you again — Auf Wiedersehen", "Good day or Good afternoon — Guten Tag"). German Wiktionary and the Regelwerk only confirm them. In review round 3 the notes on gute Nacht, tschüss, auf Wiedersehen and guten Tag, which had followed German Wiktionary's definitions, were rewritten or removed for this reason (see quality control, round 3).

Cross-checking. Every German word was looked up in German Wiktionary (calls 12: its wikitext, read with Python): spelling, part of speech, the gender of every noun against the card's article, the nominative plural, the first meaning, and its English and Swedish translations (the evidence quotes the first English and the first Swedish translation line of the entry; where those belong to a sense other than the card's, as for hallo and Straße, the evidence quotes the lines of the matching sense instead). Every English meaning was checked against the German section of English Wiktionary (calls 13). Every Swedish word was checked in Folkets lexikon (calls 14), one look-up per Swedish word on the card, English → Swedish, or Swedish → English when the first direction had no match; the look-up prefers an entry of the card's word class. The spelling points listed under the Rechtschreibrat source were checked in the official rules and word list of 2024 (call 11). A Python script built the evidence lines from the responses saved during authoring, so each quotation is what the source returned; wiki markup was rendered as plain text (links as their text, label templates such as {{K|…}} and {{ugs.}} as their names in brackets, gender markers dropped), and lists of translations longer than 140 characters were cut. The raw responses were working files and are not published; the code that read them (the Wiktionary parsing, the word-list look-up in the Regelwerk, the PDF text extraction and the Folkets matching) is recorded under queries 11, 12 and 14.

Duden and DWDS. The brief asked for each German form to be verified in Duden online or the DWDS. The DWDS terms of use (https://www.dwds.de/d/nutzungsbedingungen) say: "Jegliche Nutzung der Inhalte des DWDS, einschließlich jedoch nicht beschränkt auf automatisierte Abfragen und Auswertungen (Crawlen, Parsen, Text- und Data-Mining), sofern nicht über § 60d UrhG zulässig, ist nur mit ausdrücklicher Genehmigung gestattet." An AI agent can only consult a dictionary through automated requests, so the DWDS was not used: one entry page (https://www.dwds.de/wb/Tisch) had been fetched before the terms were read, and nothing from it is in this deck or its evidence. Duden online was not consulted either. German Wiktionary (open licence, automated access allowed) and the official spelling rules of the Rat für deutsche Rechtschreibung took their place as verification sources.

Machine checks. The dossier's Wikidata checks (270 checks on 108 items: the German label or alias of each linked item that matches the front, its English and Swedish label or alias that matches the back, the mul digit label of each number, and, since review round 3, the labels of the items behind the notes on Mann, Frau, Schwester, Januar, Straße and auf Wiedersehen: husband, wife, nurse, Austria, the Swiss Standard German label Strasse, goodbye and adjö) are re-run against live Wikidata by the builder on every build. Where an item's label does not match the card, no check was added and the difference is listed under quality control, round 0. Wikidata lexemes cannot be checked by the builder (it checks items only); the lexeme facts in the evidence were read from the API responses of 4 October 2026.

Excluded: words whose everyday form differs by region (Brötchen/Semmel, Junge/Bub, Sonnabend and Jänner, which appear only in notes), words with two equally common meanings that a single card cannot separate (Morgen/morgen: morning/tomorrow; die Bank: bench/bank), pairs a beginner cannot tell apart without context (wissen/kennen, both "to know"), the pronouns du/Sie, which need more than a flashcard, the colloquial Mama, Papa, Oma and Opa, and the colours orange, rosa and lila, which do not inflect like the others.
selection: 125 cards: the cardinal numbers 0–20, the tens 30–90 and 100 (29); the seven days of the week; the twelve months; eight colours (red, blue, green, yellow, black, white, grey, brown); eight family members (mother, father, brother, sister, son, daughter, grandfather, grandmother); twelve greetings and polite phrases (hallo, guten Morgen, guten Tag, guten Abend, gute Nacht, tschüss, auf Wiedersehen, danke, bitte, Entschuldigung, ja, nein); 25 everyday nouns (Haus, Wasser, Brot, Milch, Apfel, Buch, Tisch, Stuhl, Tür, Fenster, Hund, Katze, Stadt, Straße, Schule, Mann, Frau, Kind, Geld, Arbeit, Hand, Tag, Nacht, Jahr, Woche); eight adjectives (groß, klein, gut, schlecht, neu, alt, kalt, warm); and 16 common verbs in the infinitive (sein, haben, gehen, kommen, machen, sprechen, essen, trinken, wohnen, lesen, schreiben, schlafen, arbeiten, kaufen, sehen, sagen). The list was chosen by the deck's authors for a first course, not copied from any frequency list, textbook or phrase book. Every word has a Wikidata lexeme except guten Tag, guten Abend, gute Nacht and auf Wiedersehen, which come from the public-domain FSI course and the War Department's phrase book (guten Tag and guten Abend also from Wikidata items). The standard form common to Germany, Austria and Switzerland was chosen where one exists; where usage differs by country or region, the card gives the form standard in Germany and the note names the variant (Sonnabend, Jänner, Strasse). Left out: regional words (Brötchen/Semmel, Junge/Bub), words with two equally common meanings (Morgen, Bank), word pairs a beginner cannot tell apart on one card (wissen/kennen), the pronouns du and Sie, colloquial family words (Mama, Papa, Oma, Opa) and the uninflected colours orange, rosa and lila. The deck is studied front to back only: although no two backs are identical, the reverse direction would be ambiguous for the greetings (hello: hallo or guten Tag; bye and goodbye: tschüss or auf Wiedersehen, both hej då in Swedish).
